gold: Cold storage is a $150B global logistics segment growing about 13% a year.
Inventory counting in cold storage is manual, done in sub-zero conditions, with error rates of 4 to 8 percent.
Mid-sized operators are about 60% of the cold-storage footprint and are almost entirely unserved by automation vendors.
The serviceable market for counting and audit automation is about $2.1B.
The Larkspur robot operates reliably at -25°C, which no competing robot does.
Deployment takes under two days per facility with no changes to racking.
The software layer is where durable margin will come from.
Traction: nine paying customers across 31 facilities, up from three customers a year ago.
ARR is $1.4M with 140% net revenue retention as customers expand to more sites.
The two largest customers expanded from pilot to more than six facilities within four months.
Gross margin is 38% today and projected to reach 55% at scale.
The founders have relevant experience: the CEO ran hardware operations through an acquisition and the CTO led perception at an autonomous forklift startup.
The 22-person team includes six engineers who have shipped industrial robots, unusual for a Series A.
Incumbents have not entered cold storage because their platforms fail below freezing and the operators are too small for their sales motion.
The two seed-stage competitors lack sub -10°C units, giving Larkspur a 12 to 18 month head start.
forbidden: Hardware margins may not reach projections if component costs stay elevated (risk).
Customer concentration: top two customers are 45% of ARR (risk).
A large incumbent could build a cold-rated variant (risk).
The ask: $4M of a $12M round at $60M post.
